To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the science of uncertainty in ecology has had a very limited influence on policy making and that this is due to a number of factors, including: the limited recognition of the problem by policy makers; the lack of communication between scientists and policy makers; the limited use of ecological knowledge in policy formulation; and the failure to recognize the importance of uncertainty and ignorance in the ecological literature.

(1) the science of ecology can provide important information for policy making, but it is not well understood or utilized; (2) there is a need for improved communication and interaction between the science and the policy community; (3) there is an urgent need for improved techniques to deal with risk, uncertainty and especially ignorance, and (4) there is a strong need to develop contingency plans for the management of ecological systems

uncertainty is a key problem in the formulation of policy to address ecological issues, and that the science of risk and uncertainty is inadequate for addressing the problem of uncertainty in ecological science and policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of how to make policy decisions in the face of ignorance and uncertainty.
how to make decisions about the sustainability of ecological processes and systems in the face of uncertainty.
the role of ecology in the policy process, and the implications for ecological science of the policy process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we do not yet know how to make policy in the face of ecological uncertainty.
the science-policy interface is not working well, and that the science of ecosystems and ecology has a limited influence on the policy formulation process.
there is much work to be done in this area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the problem of uncertainty in ecology and policy is not well understood, and that the science of uncertainty and ignorance needs to be developed further.
the precautionary principle is not a sufficient response to the sustainability-uncertainty challenge, and that the challenge itself is not adequately understood.
we need to be more aware of the limitations of our knowledge, but that this is not an excuse for inaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many uncertainties and ignorances associated with ecological systems, and the policy community must recognize this and act accordingly.
there is a strong need to improve the way we communicate the uncertainties of ecological science to policy makers.
the precautionary principle and its variants have been used in a way that has not fully considered uncertainty and ignorance in ecology.
